## Author-provided scientific guidance

### Scope and use of the disclosed baseline

This guidance discloses the authors' baseline for the same substrate rearrangement and relative stereochemical question stated in the task. Execute and critically assess that baseline, documenting fidelity, ambiguities, and scientifically justified substitutions in the existing investigation records and report. The quoted diagnostic controls and observations on other compounds are background to the authors' reasoning, not new inputs to fit, required experiments, extra scientific goals, or additional deliverables. Do not assert that a substituted model is numerically identical to the disclosed one.

### Author-reported diagnostic hypothesis support, verbatim

To elucidate the mechanism of this unprecedented skeletal rearrangement, a series of experiments was conducted. The addition of 2,2,6,6-tetramethylpiperidine-1-oxyl (TEMPO), DMPO (5,5-dimethyl-1-pyrroline N-oxide) or BHT (butylated hydroxytoluene) suppressed the reaction significantly under the standard conditions (Figure 3A, entries 2 \mathrm { ~ - ~ } 4 )

### Author-reported mechanism, computed results and interpretation, verbatim

Moreover, the DMPO-1a and BHT-1a adducts could be detected by HRMS (Supporting Information). These results indicate a radical-mediated mechanism. The reaction was significantly inhibited by triplet-state quenchers, including oxygen and, particularly, the conjugated hexa-2,4-diene, suggesting the involvement of an energy transfer process (entries 5 7). Furthermore, the UV–vis absorption spectrum displayed a linear Stern–Volmer plot with a positive slope (Figure 3B), confirming the quenching the triplet TXO by 1a. Notably, the reaction of enantiopure 1a (>99% ee) proceeded with complete loss of chirality, suggesting rapid racemization of a carbon-centered intermediate (Figure 3C). To further elucidate the mechanistic details of the transformation, we conducted density functional theory (DFT) calculations with model substrate 1a (Figure 3D). DFT calculations reveal that photoexcited TXO ( \mathrm { E _ { T } } ~ = ~ 6 5 . 5 kcal/mol) efficiently transfers its energy to 1a ( \mathrm { E _ { T } = 5 2 . 2 \ k c a l / m o l ) } , generating the triplet diradical <sup>3</sup>1a via excitation of the C═C moiety. In contrast, excitation of the C═O moiety is precluded because its triplet energy (75.6 kcal/mol) is significantly higher than that of TXO, ruling out the Norrish-type reaction pathway under the present conditions.<sup>[52,53]</sup> On the triplet potential energy surface, <sup>3</sup>1a undergoes a 5-exo-trig radical addition to the carbonyl moiety via transition state TS1, with an activation Gibbs energy of 9.7 kcal/mol, forming a bicyclic intermediate <sup>3</sup>A. This pathway is kinetically favored over the competing 1,5-hydrogen atom transfer (1,5-HAT) process, which exhibits a higher activation Gibbs energy (12.1 kcal/mol). Subsequent C─C bond cleavage of the dirad ical species <sup>3</sup>A proceeds through TS2 with a low activation Gibbs energy (3.0 kcal/mol), generating an eight-membered diradical intermediate <sup>3</sup>B ( \Delta \mathbf { G } = - 1 3 . 6 \mathrm { k c a l / m o l } ) . Minimum energy crossing point (MECP) calculations were performed using the sobMECP software to estimate the minimum electronic energy required for intersystem crossing (ISC) during closure of ring-forming step. DFT calculations predict that the generation of cis-2 is favored, as the cis-configured MECP \left( \mathbf { M E C P } _ { c i s } \right) lies about 3.7 kcal/mol lower in electronic energy that \mathbf { M E C P } _ { t r a n s } , aligning with the experimental observations. Moreover, cis-2 is thermodynamically more stable than trans-2 by 23.5 kcal/mol, indicating that the severe strain in the trans-product drives thermal isomerization.<sup>[54,55]</sup> Accordingly, control experiments with products 22 and 27 ( \Delta \mathrm { G } = 1 4 . 2 ~ / 11.2 kcal/mol for trans-22 / 27 relative to cis-22 / 27), which were initially obtained as a 1:1 mixture of diastereomers, showed that the dr ratio remained unchanged when the mixture was stirred at room temperature for 12 h in the dark. However, upon heating \mathrm { t o 8 0 ^ { \circ } C } , excellent diastereoselectivity was obtained, in support of thermal isomerization of the highly strained trans-isomer (Figure 3E).

### Author-performed computational procedure, verbatim

All calculations were carried out using density functional-theory (DFT) with Gaussian 16.<sup>[18]</sup> The geometry optimizations were performed with the ωB97X-D<sup>[19]</sup> functional using def2-SVP<sup>[20]</sup> basis set in DMSO using SMD<sup>[21]</sup> solvation model at room temperature. Frequency calculations performed at the same level of theory were used to classify each stationary point. Geometries without imaginary frequencies were deemed minima and those with only one imaginary frequency along the chemical path of interest were deemed transition states. Single point energies were carried out at the ωB97X-D / def2-TZVP<sup>[22]</sup> / SMD (DMSO) level of theory. To obtain more accurate Gibbs free energy (G) and enthalpies (H), we applied the quasi-harmonic approximation from Grimme<sup>[23]</sup> to compute the thermal corrections with a cut-off frequency of 1 0 0 ~ \mathrm { { c m } ^ { - 1 } } , thereby providing the final G and H in Shermo propram<sup>[24]</sup>. Minimum energy crossing points (MECP) were located using sobMECP program<sup>[25]</sup> interfaced with Gaussian 16. Conformational search using ABCluster program<sup>[26]</sup> was conducted to ensure that the conformers we reported were in their lowest energy conformation. The 20 conformers (if there are) with the lowest energy obtained from ABCluster were then optimized by DFT to determine the most stable conformer. The 3D diagrams of optimized structures were generated with CYLview20 software<sup>[27]</sup>.

### Author computational figure caption, verbatim

Figure 3. A) Radical trapping and triplet energy quenching experiments. B) Stern-Volmer fluorescence quenching. C) Stereoselectivity observation of the reaction. D) Computational studies. Calculations were performed at SMD(solvent DMSO)/(U)ωB97X-D/def2tzvp//(U)ωB97X-D/def2svp leve of theory. (E) Thermodynamic experiments.

### Source-bound numerical figure reading, not an author prose quotation

Reviewer visual interpretation (not a verbatim source quotation): Figure 3D explicitly distinguishes Gibbs energies from parenthesized electronic energies. Relative to triplet 1a=0, singlet 1a is -52.2 in ΔG (-56.8 in ΔE); TS1 is 9.7 (8.2); cis and trans MECP electronic energies are -12.4 and -8.7. Products cis-2 and trans-2 have ΔG=-48.9 and -25.4, respectively. Therefore cis MECP is lower by 3.7 in electronic energy and cis product lower by 23.5 in Gibbs free energy. HAT TS1' appears at 12.2 in the figure but 12.1 in prose; it is excluded from the reference subset.

### Connectivity and additional displayed model context

In the displayed author route, the terminal allyl carbon adds to the ketone carbonyl carbon, giving the bicyclic radical-addition intermediate. Cleavage of the original bond between the ketone carbonyl carbon and the ester-bearing ring carbon gives the eight-membered diradical; closure bonds the ester-bearing carbon to the phenyl-bearing former alkene carbon. The main figure calls the two crossing arrangements syn/anti, while the supplementary figure calls them cis/trans and connects them to the corresponding products. The supplementary energy diagram also shows the competing hydrogen-transfer intermediate labelled 3C at -5.7 in Gibbs energy (-5.3 electronic) and HAT crossing points at electronic relative energies 3.9 and 6.0 kcal/mol. These contextual branches are disclosed as performed author work, not added independent goals or a requirement to reconstruct a complete reaction network.

### Source discrepancies retained rather than silently reconciled

The main prose reports the competing HAT barrier as 12.1 kcal/mol, whereas the main and supplementary diagrams label it 12.2. The main prose places the intermediate 3B at -13.6 kcal/mol, whereas both diagrams label it -14.4 in Gibbs energy (-17.5 electronic). These discrepancies are preserved; neither value pair is a strict scoring target. The four coherent frozen comparisons concern the substrate separation, first addition barrier, cis/trans crossing ordering, and cis/trans product ordering, not a demand for agreement with every diagram label.

### Interpretation and protocol limitations

The substrate's reported 52.2 kcal/mol singlet-to-triplet separation is the Gibbs-energy separation in the displayed profile; 56.8 is the parenthesized electronic separation. It is not a measured or vertical electronic excitation energy. The quoted 65.5 kcal/mol sensitizer benchmark is contextual, not an author-computed substrate reference. The 3.7 crossing preference is an electronic-energy ordering, not a Gibbs activation barrier or an independently computed intersystem-crossing rate. The 23.5 product preference is a Gibbs-energy ordering, not by itself an isomerization rate. The thermal controls quoted above concern products 22 and 27 rather than the model product 2. The procedure states room temperature without a numerical temperature in the quoted method block, reports frequency-based stationary-point classification without an explicit IRC protocol there, and reports no numerical uncertainty interval for these comparison values. This guidance does not supply original Gaussian input decks or complete execution logs. Prepare inputs from the shared molecular identities, state any necessary assumptions, and document rather than invent unavailable settings or validation. Neither the author interpretation nor numerical agreement alone establishes a unique mechanism.
